blogs.title: Procedural Rights Without Remedies: The D.C. Circuit Tightens Standing in OSC–FOIA Disputes
blogs.description: The panel’s core holding is a standing opinion with teeth. Even assuming § 1216 imposes a duty on OSC to investigate arbitrary FOIA withholdings, the court finds no Article III injury or redressability. The opinion rejects two informational-injury theories: (1) that an OSC investigation would lead—through a speculative chain involving OSC, MSPB, and DOJ—to production of DOJ records; and (2) that § 1216 investigations entitle requesters to § 1214-style notices. Leaning on Summers, Akins, and Public Citizen, and more recent causation/redressability authorities (Haaland, Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, Hecate Energy), the court emphasizes independent-actor breaks in the causal chain and the absence of any statutory entitlement to information from an OSC § 1216 probe. The piece will unpack how the panel applies the “relaxed” procedural-injury framework while insisting on a concrete interest and likely redress—signaling limited room for watchdogs to leverage downstream enforcement processes as a basis for standing.

blogs.title: The Merits That Weren’t: Unresolved Tensions Between § 1216, § 552(a)(4)(F), and § 1214
blogs.description: The district court said OSC legally erred by treating FOIA’s § 552(a)(4)(F) predicates as a precondition to any § 1216 investigation, but the D.C. Circuit vacated on standing and never reached that merits question. This post maps the statutory puzzle: whether § 1216(a)(3)’s “shall conduct an investigation” language operates independently of FOIA’s post-litigation disciplinary trigger, and if so, whether and when § 1214’s notification procedures attach to a § 1216 investigation. We’ll situate the district court’s reading against Carson (6th Cir.) and the panel’s hints about OSC discretion, identifying the open issues now teed up for a future plaintiff who can clear standing—particularly the scope of any mandatory investigative duty and the portability (or not) of § 1214’s process to § 1216 matters.

blogs.title: Heckler in the Background: Why Courts Won’t Compel OSC’s FOIA Policing
blogs.description: This case showcases the gravitational pull of enforcement-discretion doctrine. The court stresses that standing cannot rest on speculation about how OSC would wield its prosecutorial choices, invoking Heckler v. Chaney. We explore how Chaney shapes both causation (because discretionary steps break the chain) and redressability (because courts won’t order an investigation that may go nowhere), especially when multiple independent actors (OSC, MSPB, DOJ) control outcomes. The post will also compare OSC’s discretion over § 1216 investigations to its established roles in prohibited-personnel-practice cases, and examine the institutional reasons appellate courts bridle at turning investigatory ‘shall’ language into judicially enforceable commands.

blogs.title: FOIA Watchdogs After AFL v. Greer: A Litigation Playbook That Survives Standing
blogs.description: What can requesters do post-decision? This practical guide outlines viable routes: (1) pursue standard FOIA litigation for agency records rather than trying to conscript OSC; (2) leverage § 552(a)(4)(F) by seeking a judicial order, fee award, and an express finding that an agency acted arbitrarily or capriciously—thereby triggering OSC’s separate mandatory initiation; (3) if targeting OSC, identify a statutory entitlement to information (not just an investigation) to ground informational standing; and (4) develop non-speculative theories of redress that do not hinge on multiple independent actors. We’ll flag evidentiary strategies for establishing concrete injury and likely redress and note where organizational-plaintiff allegations typically fall short under the D.C. Circuit’s framework.
